title: What a Realistic Weekly Schedule Looks Like in IA…
summary: See what a realistic weekly schedule looks like during IB DP2 IA season, with a September-November plan for coursework, revision, sleep, and rest.
body_markdown:
A realistic IA-season schedule does not assign every free hour to coursework. During the **IB DP2 fall term** , a sustainable week usually contains **4-6 focused IA hours** , regular homework and subject review, protected rest, and enough flexibility to absorb an experiment problem or unexpected deadline.


The balance depends on your subjects and school calendar. This September-November model suits students who are collecting evidence, drafting analysis, receiving feedback, and managing overlapping coursework.


### Start With Your School Deadlines


Most Diploma Programme subjects include assessment completed during the course, such as investigations, oral work, fieldwork, and practical work. Some components are marked by teachers and moderated by the IB, while others are externally assessed. The[IB overview of Diploma Programme assessment](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/) explains these arrangements.


There is no single student-facing IA calendar used identically by every IB World School. Your teachers and DP coordinator set internal checkpoints and submission dates, so those dates should control your schedule. Ask for the first-draft date, feedback window, final school deadline, and any earlier checkpoints.


Place every deadline on one page, then label each IA by stage:


- **Focus:** finalizing the question, aim, text, case study, or topic
- **Evidence:** collecting sources, experimental data, observations, or calculations
- **Analysis:** interpreting findings and connecting them to the question
- **Drafting:** assembling sections into a complete response
- **Revision:** applying feedback and checking technical requirements


Stages are more useful than a vague instruction such as *work on Chemistry IA* . The[RevisionDojo IA planning guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-plan-an-ib-ia-without-falling-behind) shows how to convert a large assessment into measurable outputs.


### What a Realistic Weekly Schedule Looks Like


This model provides about **5-6 hours of deliberate IA work** , alongside subject maintenance and ordinary homework. Teacher-assigned work may require extra time, but it should not automatically replace sleep or every rest period.


Day Main block Secondary block Purpose


Monday 60-minute priority IA block 45 minutes of homework Produce one defined output


Tuesday 90-minute IA block 15-20 minutes of recall Complete analysis, calculations, or drafting


Wednesday 60 minutes of homework 30 minutes of IA administration Organize citations, figures, files, or questions


Thursday 90-minute IA block 30 minutes of exam practice Produce the main weekly deliverable


Friday Rest or 30-minute emergency buffer None Prevent work consuming the weekend


Saturday Two 60-minute IA blocks 45 minutes of timed practice Complete concentration-heavy work


Sunday 45 minutes of light IA work 60 minutes of homework and planning Close loose ends and set the next milestone


This is practical advice, not an official IB requirement. Adjust it around laboratories, sport, employment, commuting, family responsibilities, and your concentration patterns.


Keep **one IA in deep-work mode** and another in **maintenance mode** . Biology might receive the Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday blocks, while Economics receives Wednesday's citation check. Attempting major progress on three IAs in one evening usually creates fragmented work.


### How the Schedule Changes From September to November


### September: establish control


Confirm deadlines, test whether topics are feasible, identify required evidence, and reserve access to laboratories, participants, texts, databases, or equipment. Each block should create an observable result, such as an approved question, pilot dataset, annotated source list, method draft, or outline.


The[RevisionDojo guide to managing IA time](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/time-management-strategies-for-completing-your-ia-on-schedule) explains how concrete mini-deadlines make distant final deadlines manageable.


### October: prioritize evidence and analysis


Normal teaching continues while coursework becomes more substantial. Use deep-work blocks for genuine production tasks, including processing results, comparing sources, performing calculations, or drafting arguments.


Retain at least two short revision sessions weekly. Retrieve definitions, complete a small question set, and record errors rather than attempting complete units. The[guide to combining IAs and revision](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/the-role-of-internal-assessments-ias-and-revision-how-to-integrate-them-into-your-study-routine) explains how subject practice can continue without dominating the IA schedule.


### November: revise and submit


An IA approaching submission should shift from content creation to revision. Translate each teacher comment into an action. Instead of *improve evaluation* , write: identify two limitations, explain how each affected the findings, and propose a feasible improvement.


The[RevisionDojo IA feedback guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-internal-assessment-feedback-detailed-comments-and-suggestions) provides a framework for connecting comments to assessment criteria. Where possible, keep a **48-72 hour personal buffer** for references, figure labels, word limits, forms, file checks, and submission instructions.


### Protect Exam Readiness


IA season should not eliminate exam preparation. A manageable minimum is **15-25 minutes of retrieval practice on 4 days** , plus one **30-45 minute exam-style session** weekly.


A maintenance session can include five minutes recalling a topic without notes, twenty minutes answering targeted questions, and five minutes recording a recurring mistake. The[RevisionDojo IB resources hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib) provides Study Notes, Flashcards, and the Questionbank for focused sessions. The aim is to keep older content accessible, not create a second full study schedule.


### Make Every IA Block Produce Something Visible


Define the intended output before starting.


Weak task Executable task


Work on History IA Annotate four pieces of evidence for Section B


Do Biology analysis Process trial data and produce one labelled graph


Fix Mathematics IA Explain the model result and check two calculations


Sort references Add missing details and check in-text citations


Afterward, save the file clearly and record the next action. This reduces time lost when restarting.


Use Jojo AI or feedback tools to clarify criteria, organize comments, and identify questions, not to generate assessed writing for submission. The IB requires AI-generated material to be handled transparently under academic integrity expectations. Read the[IB guidance on artificial intelligence in assessment](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-learning-teaching-and-assessment/) and follow your school's policy.


### Warning Signs That the Schedule Is Unrealistic


Revise your plan if:


- You schedule more than **3 hours of demanding work** after school.
- Every weekday contains deep work with no recovery evening.
- IA work removes exam practice for several weeks.
- Tasks repeatedly move forward because they lack defined outputs.
- Friday or Sunday night must rescue the whole week.
- Sleep is shortened to compensate for poor estimates.


Reduce scope before increasing hours. Check whether the question is too broad, the method unnecessarily complicated, or formatting is being polished before analysis is complete. Contact your teacher early if data, equipment, health, or access problems threaten a deadline.


### Conclusion


A realistic weekly schedule during IA season contains a few protected deep-work blocks, one main coursework priority, short revision anchors, and genuine recovery time. September establishes direction, October emphasizes evidence and analysis, and November focuses on feedback and submission checks.


RevisionDojo can support this structure through Jojo AI, the Questionbank, Flashcards, Study Notes, and IA Feedback, but the thinking and submitted work must remain your own. Begin with IA planning or Coursework Review, then use short Questionbank and Flashcard sessions to maintain exam readiness.
